articles.title: Dashain and Tihar of Nepal: A Comprehensive Historical and Cultural Study
articles.subtitle: An in-depth reference on the origins, mythology, rituals, regional variations, political history and modern transformation of Nepal's two greatest festivals
articles.author: SUJAN
articles.body:
Dashain (Bada Dashain, Bijaya Dashami) and Tihar (Deepawali, Yamapanchak, Swanti) form the twin pillars of Nepal's festival calendar. Falling in the autumn months of Ashwin and Kartik, they bind together religion, kinship, statecraft, agriculture, commerce and migration into a single annual cycle of renewal. Dashain, a fifteen-day festival devoted to the Goddess Durga and the triumph of dharma over adharma, is the longest and most widely observed national holiday. Tihar, a five-day festival of lights, honours Yama, the crow, the dog, the cow, the ox, Goddess Laxmi and, uniquely, the bond between brothers and sisters. This study traces both festivals from their textual and mythological roots in the Vedic and Puranic traditions, through their consolidation under the Malla and Shah dynasties, the Rana regime and the Panchayat era, to their experience in the modern republic and the global Nepali diaspora. It also examines the critical debates that surround them: animal sacrifice, caste, indigenous identity, consumption and labour migration.

Part One: Foundations

1.1 The Calendar Behind the Festivals To understand when Dashain and Tihar occur, one must understand the calendar that governs them. Nepal's religious life follows a lunisolar system in which months are counted by the moon but are periodically corrected to keep pace with the sun's seasonal cycle. Each lunar month is divided into two fortnights: the Shukla Paksha (bright half, waxing moon, ending in the full moon or Purnima) and the Krishna Paksha (dark half, waning moon, ending in the new moon or Aunsi). Days within each fortnight are called tithis.

The civil calendar of Nepal is the Bikram Sambat (B.S.), a solar calendar that runs roughly 56 years and eight months ahead of the Gregorian calendar. Religious observances, however, are fixed by the lunar panchang (almanac), compiled by astrologers who calculate the auspicious moments, called sait, for every ritual. This is why Dashain and Tihar move across the Gregorian calendar each year, usually falling between late September and mid-November. Dashain is observed in the lunar month of Ashwin (Ashwayuja), from the first day of the bright fortnight (Shukla Pratipada) to the full moon (Purnima), with its climax on the tenth day (Dashami). Tihar is observed in Kartik, beginning on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight (Krishna Trayodashi) and ending on the second day of the following bright fortnight (Shukla Dwitiya). The interval between the two festivals is therefore roughly three to four weeks: the first is the festival of the Goddess, power and victory; the second is the festival of light, prosperity and family.

1.2 The Agricultural Rhythm Both festivals sit at the hinge of the agrarian year. The monsoon has ended, the rice (dhan) is ripening or being harvested in the Tarai and the mid-hills, and the clear autumn skies have returned. This timing is not incidental. Scholars of South Asian religion have long argued that autumn goddess festivals incorporate older harvest and fertility rites. The ritual sowing of barley shoots (jamara) at the start of Dashain, and the later offering of rice, new grain and fruit, point to a deep agricultural substrate beneath the narrative layers of myth. Tihar's celebration of the cow, the ox and Laxmi, the goddess of wealth, similarly reflects a cattle-based farming economy in which animals and grain were literal sources of prosperity.

1.3 Etymology The word Dashain (also spelled Dasain) is the Nepali form of the Sanskrit Dashami, 'the tenth', referring to the tenth day when the festival reaches its peak. It is called Bijaya Dashami ('the tenth day of victory'), and Bada Dashain ('Great Dashain') to distinguish it from lesser observances. In the Newar community, it is known as Mohani. Elsewhere in India the same festival complex is known as Dussehra, Navaratri or Durga Puja.

Tihar is the Nepali name, often translated as 'festival of lights'. Its other names include Deepawali or Deewali (from Sanskrit dipavali, a row of lamps), Yamapanchak (the five days of Yama), and in Newar, Swanti.

Part Two: Dashain

2.1 Mythological and Textual Roots Dashain draws upon at least four distinct narrative strands, which have merged over centuries into a single festival. First, the Devi Mahatmya. The foundational text of Shakta Hinduism is the Devi Mahatmya (also called the Durga Saptashati or Chandi), a section of the Markandeya Purana usually dated between the fifth and sixth centuries CE. It tells how the buffalodemon Mahishasura, having received a boon that no man or god could kill him, conquered heaven and displaced the gods. The gods, in despair, combined their energies (tejas) to create a supreme feminine power, Durga, armed with the weapons of all the gods. After a prolonged battle, traditionally counted as nine nights, she slew Mahishasura on the tenth day. This is the primary mythic template for Navaratri, 'the nine nights', and for Vijaya Dashami, 'the day of victory'. Durga here is not the subordinate consort of a male god but the ultimate source of cosmic power (Shakti), a theological assertion that was transformative in the history of Indian religion. Second, the Ramayana. In the Rama tradition, Rama, preparing for his war against the demon-king Ravana, invoked the goddess Durga out of season in autumn (an act known in Bengali tradition as akal bodhan, 'untimely awakening') to obtain her blessing. Rama defeated and killed Ravana on the tenth day. This narrative is the basis of the Dussehra celebrations of North India, where effigies of Ravana are burned. It is also why many Nepalis understand Dashain as the triumph of good over evil in a general sense. Third, the Mahabharata. The epic tells how the Pandavas, during the final year of their exile, hid their divine weapons in a shami tree and recovered them at the end of the year of concealment, using them to win victory. The Shami Puja (worship of the shami tree) and the practice of worshipping weapons (Ayudha Puja) on Vijaya Dashami derive from this episode. Military significance became a central feature of Dashain in Nepal, as we shall see.

Fourth, folk and local traditions. Beneath these pan-Indian narratives lies a layer of local goddess worship, including the worship of mother goddesses (Matrika), clan goddesses (Kuladevi), and the Newar tantric deities, which fused with the Puranic Durga cult. The Nepali Dashain is therefore as much a local synthesis as an import.

2.2 Early History in the Himalaya Direct documentary evidence for the precise form of Dashain in early Nepal is limited, and scholars should be cautious about claims of exact origins. Several things can be said with reasonable confidence. During the Licchavi period (roughly the fourth to ninth centuries CE), inscriptions and sculpture from the Kathmandu Valley show strong Shaiva, Vaishnava and Shakta devotion, including sculptural depictions of Mahishasuramardini (Durga slaying the buffalo demon). Images of the goddess in this form from Licchavi-era sites indicate that her cult was established in the valley. Licchavi kings also sponsored festivals, and the worship of goddesses was a recognised part of royal religion. The Malla period (broadly the 12th to 18th centuries) is where the state-sponsored Dashain becomes clearly visible. A key moment in the tradition is the arrival of the goddess Taleju Bhawani. Tradition holds that the deity was brought to the valley by Harisimhadeva of Simraungarh in the early fourteenth century (usually dated to about 1324 CE), after his flight from the Tughluq advance into the Tarai. Taleju became the tutelary deity (Ishta-devata) of the Malla kings and, through them, of Kathmandu, Bhaktapur and Patan. Temples to Taleju were constructed in the royal palace complexes; the Taleju temple of Kathmandu's Hanuman Dhoka palace, built in the sixteenth century, remains among the tallest and most sacred temple structures in the city. Access to the Taleju shrine was restricted to initiated worshippers and the royal household throughout the year, and is opened to the general public only on Maha Navami, a practice that continues today. Under the Mallas, Dashain was a state festival, involving royal sacrifices, military review, the display of arms, and the reaffirmation of the bond between ruler and goddess. The king, as the earthly representative of the goddess's protection, received her blessing and then, in turn, distributed blessings to the court and the people.

2.3 The Shah Dynasty and the Gorkhali State The unification of Nepal in the late eighteenth century profoundly shaped Dashain's character. The Shah rulers of Gorkha, led by Prithvi Narayan Shah, who conquered the Kathmandu Valley in 1768–69, carried with them their own state-goddess cult centred on Gorkha Kalika and the royal palace at Gorkha. After the conquest they merged the Gorkhali traditions with those of the valley, adopting Taleju and the valley's royal rituals while retaining the Gorkha Kalika connection. The practice of Phulpati (see below) carries this memory: the sacred offering that is carried each year from the Gorkha palace to Kathmandu. Prithvi Narayan Shah's famous description of Nepal as a 'true Hindu land' and the later codification of a Hindu social order, culminating in the Muluki Ain of 1854 under Jang Bahadur Rana, tied the observance of Hindu festivals, Dashain above all, to state identity. Dashain became a vehicle for the integration of a diverse kingdom around the figure of the monarch and a shared set of Hindu symbols. The king gave tika to the nation's elites at the palace, military officers, civil servants and local notables received it in turn, and the royal blessing flowed outward through the hierarchy. The Rana period (1846–1951) made Dashain a spectacular display of state and military power. The prime ministerial family hosted elaborate ceremonies, animal sacrifices on a large scale were offered at the Kot to weapons and military standards, and parades were held at the Tundikhel parade ground. Ritual and martial display were fused.

2.4 The Panchayat Era, Democracy and the Republic The fall of the Rana regime in 1951 and the return of direct royal power, followed by the Panchayat system (1960–1990), kept Dashain firmly tied to the monarchy. The king's tika at the palace and his Dashain address stood as markers of the national-Hindu identity that the Panchayat regime promoted. After the restoration of multiparty democracy in 1990, and especially after the 2006 People's Movement (Jana Andolan II) and the abolition of the monarchy in 2008, Nepal became a secular federal republic. Dashain, however, retained its position as a national public holiday. The ceremonial tika at the head of state's residence is now given by the President, who receives guests and gives tika to senior officials and the public. The continuity of the festival through changes of regime shows how deeply it is rooted in Nepali social life beyond any single political order.

2.5 The Fifteen Days: Ritual Structure The festival runs from the first day of the bright fortnight of Ashwin to the full moon. Not all fifteen days are equally observed, but the main stages are as follows.

Day 1: Ghatasthapana Ghatasthapana ('establishing the vessel') opens the festival. At the auspicious moment, the household's priest or senior member sets up a kalash (a sacred water vessel) in the family's prayer room, the Dashain Ghar, and invokes Goddess Durga into it. A small bed of sand or soil mixed with cow dung is prepared, and barley seeds (sometimes mixed with other grains) are sown around the vessel. This is the origin of the jamara, the yellow sprouts that will later be worn on the head. The vessel is kept covered and shielded from direct sunlight, and watered each morning and evening through the festival. The jamara's growth is read as an omen of the household's fortune.

Days 2–6: Navaratri Observance For the nine nights of Navaratri, devotees worship the nine forms of Durga, the Navadurga. Many people, particularly women, visit Durga temples before dawn, fast, and read the Devi Mahatmya or Durga Saptashati. Popular pilgrimage destinations include Dakshinkali, Guhyeshwari, Shobha Bhagwati, Bhadrakali, and the temples of Pharping and Manakamana, as well as the Gorkha Kalika.

Day 7: Phulpati Phulpati ('flowers and leaves') is the seventh-day ritual in which the sacred kalash, a bundle of leaves and plants, jamara and a sugarcane stalk tied with a red cloth, is brought in procession to the Hanuman Dhoka Durbar in Kathmandu. Historically, the Phulpati was carried from the royal palace at Gorkha, a journey of several days on foot. Today, the main procession is carried by designated bearers, accompanied by a military band and a ceremonial guard, and the entry into Kathmandu is attended by senior officials and large crowds. The ritual plants (the banana, jayanti, bel and others, representing the elements of the nine-plant Navapatrika, in which Durga is symbolically present) carry forward the idea that the goddess dwells in nature itself.

Day 8: Maha Ashtami Maha Ashtami is regarded as the most intense night of the goddess's worship. It is associated with the fiercest form of Durga, Kali, and in tantric tradition, the night (Kalratri) is the occasion of the most powerful rites. Animal offerings, which have long

Day 9: Maha Navami Maha Navami is the day of the greatest mass sacrifice. It is the day that the goddess is said to have slain Mahishasura and, in Nepali practice, also the day on which tools, vehicles and instruments are worshipped as embodiments of Durga's power. Trucks, buses, cars, motorcycles and machinery are decorated with flowers, marigolds and red tika, and are offered the blood of a chicken or goat in some traditions. This links to Vishwakarma worship, honouring the divine artisan. As previously noted, on this day the Taleju Bhawani temple in Kathmandu opens its doors to the public, drawing large crowds. In the Newar community, the Navadurga masked dancers of Bhaktapur enact the descent of the nine goddesses accompanied by the god Bhairav and other attendants.

Day 10: Vijaya Dashami Vijaya Dashami is the festival's climax, the day of victory. At the astrologically determined moment, the senior member of the household prepares the tika, a mixture of rice, yoghurt and red vermilion, and applies it to the foreheads of the younger members, together with a few jamara shoots placed behind the ears or on the head. The tika is accompanied by blessings (ashirwad) for health, prosperity and long life, and by gifts of money (dakshina). The ritual continues in descending order of age, with younger family members seeking out their elders, and visiting relatives, sometimes across great distances. The red colour of the tika, associated with the goddess's energy and the blood of the slain demon, is a visible mark of her protection.

Days 11–15: Continuation and Kojagrat Purnima For the days following Dashami, families continue the visits, receiving tika and blessings, until the full moon day. The fifteenth day, Kojagrat Purnima ('who is awake?'), is the night of Goddess Laxmi, who in tradition descends to bless those who remain awake and vigilant. It is observed with fasting, vigils, and in some households, the playing of games of chance. It is also the day on which the family's tika-giving customarily ends, and, in the Newar tradition, the formal end of Mohani.

2.6 The Tika and Social Structure The tika ritual is not merely religious. It reaffirms the relationships and hierarchies of the extended family and community. The sequence of giving and receiving encodes seniority, kinship and respect. A person who cannot travel to receive tika may send gifts or call by telephone, and the failure to maintain such relationships is felt as a significant social breach. One of the most important effects of Dashain is its role in drawing migrants home. Millions of Nepalis who work in Kathmandu, India, the Gulf states and Malaysia travel to their villages for Dashain. The festival period sees record passenger numbers on highways and in the airports, and the capital's population is visibly reduced.

2.7 Food, Dress and Recreation Dashain is a festival of abundance. The central food is meat, most commonly goat (khasi), prepared in curries and distributed after the sacrificial offering as prasad. Households also prepare fried breads and sweets, and fresh rice and vegetables. New clothes, bought especially for the festival, are worn for the tika ceremony. Two recreations are particularly associated with Dashain. The first is the bamboo swing (ping), built at village crossroads and open spaces from the start of the festival and taken down shortly after Purnima. Large, handmade, communal structures of bamboo and rope, the ping is associated with the festival's joy and is widely celebrated in folk songs. The second is kite flying, which fills the clear autumn skies, with kites of all sizes competing and being cut loose. Playing cards, although controversial, are also part of the festival's traditions in many communities.

2.8 Newar Mohani and Other Communities The Newar of the Kathmandu Valley celebrate Dashain as Mohani, with rituals distinct from those of the hill Brahmin-Chhetri communities. The key elements include the worship of the Nine Durgas (Nava Durga) and the Taleju goddess; the use of the Newar tantric tradition; and the Nawa Durga Gana, the masked dance performed in Bhaktapur, in which dancers embody the nine forms of the goddess in a ritual that is among the oldest living traditions of the valley. Newar families celebrate with their own feast, which includes samay baji and other characteristic foods. Other communities, including the Tamang, Magar, Gurung, Tharu and Madheshi groups, celebrate Dashain with local features and, in some cases, with different interpretations. Some indigenous (Janajati) communities and Buddhist groups have historically

2.9 Critical Perspectives A thorough account of Dashain must include the debates that surround it. Animal sacrifice. The sacrifice of goats, buffaloes, chickens and ducks is a central feature of Dashain in many communities. Animal-rights groups, Buddhist and Vaishnava voices and some reformist Hindus have called for an end to the practice, while supporters argue that it is an ancient religious tradition. The debate has been extensively discussed in the public sphere, and practices vary widely across communities. National identity and indigenous critique. Some scholars and indigenous activists have argued that the state's promotion of Dashain as a single national festival reflected the dominance of the hill-Hindu Khas elite and the imposition of one religious calendar on a plural society. The 1854 legal code, they note, ranked communities within a Hindu caste hierarchy. This critique has been part of the wider debate on inclusion, secularism and federalism that followed 2006. Caste and exclusion. Historically, the tika ritual has also reflected caste divisions. Reports of Dalit communities being denied entry to temples or being excluded from festival activities continue to be documented by human rights organisations, even though castebased discrimination is now illegal. Economic burden. The expectation of new clothes, gifts and feasts can create financial pressure on poor households, and loan-taking during the festival season is widely reported. The festival's economy also sees a surge of consumer spending, remittance flows and demand for livestock and goods, much of it met by imports.

Part Three: Tihar

3.1 Origins and Meaning Tihar is a Nepali festival of lights that combines several distinct traditions: the Hindu cult of Yama (the god of death), the worship of animals as divine beings, the worship of Laxmi, the Krishna tradition of Govardhan Puja, and the Newar tradition of Mha Puja. It is related to the pan-Indian Diwali (Deepawali) but has its own distinctive character, including a shorter and different order of observance and the unique emphasis on animals.

3.2 Mythological Strands Yama and Yamuna. The central narrative of the final day, Bhai Tika, tells of the god of death, Yama, who visited his sister Yamuna (the river goddess), who honoured him with a tika and a feast and prayed for his long life. Yama, pleased, declared that any brother who receives a tika from his sister on that day would be protected from untimely death. This is the origin of Bhai Tika, and also of the alternative names for the festival: Yama Dwitiya and Yamapanchak. Laxmi and the churning of the ocean. The goddess Laxmi, consort of Vishnu and goddess of wealth and prosperity, is believed to have emerged from the ocean during the cosmic churning of the ocean of milk (Samudra Manthan). On the night of the new moon (Aunsi) in Kartik, she is said to visit the world and enter homes that are clean, well lit and welcoming. The lamps lit in every doorway are a guide for her. King Bali. In the tradition connected with Diwali throughout South Asia, the god Vishnu in his dwarf avatar (Vamana) humbled the demon king Bali and sent him to the underworld, granting him the right to return once a year. The day after Laxmi Puja is sometimes known as Bali Pratipada. Krishna and Govardhan. In the Bhagavata Purana tradition, the young Krishna defended the people of Vrindavan from the wrath of the god Indra by lifting the Govardhan hill, sheltering the cattle and the villagers. The worship of the ox and of cow-dung hills (Govardhan Puja) on the fourth day commemorates this narrative. Mha Puja and Nepal Sambat. In the Newar community, the fourth day is the Mha Puja, the 'worship of the self', in which each person worships his or her own body and soul. It is also the New Year of the Nepal Sambat calendar. Tradition attributes the beginning of the era to the merchant Sankhadhar Sakhwa of Kathmandu, who, according to Newar tradition, paid off the debts of the people of the valley, leading to the inauguration of a new era in 879–880 CE. The Nepal Sambat has been a matter of cultural and political pride for the Newar community and has gained increasing official recognition in recent years.

3.3 The Five Days

Day 1: Kaag Tihar (Worship of the Crow) On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Kartik, the crow (kaag) and the raven are worshipped. Crows are seen as messengers of Yama, and their cawing is associated with grief, death or bad news. Offering them food, usually rice and sweets, placed on rooftops

Day 2: Kukur Tihar (Worship of the Dog) On the following day, the dog (kukur) is worshipped. In Hindu tradition, Yama has two foureyed dogs as guardians of the gates of the underworld, and the dog is also the messenger and vehicle of Bhairav. Dogs, whether domestic or stray, receive garlands of marigold, a red tika on the forehead and special food, in recognition of their loyalty and their role as protector. This day, unusual among the world's festivals, has attracted international attention and has become a symbol of Nepal's tradition of compassion towards animals.

Day 3: Gai Tihar and Laxmi Puja The third day, the new moon, has two parts. In the morning, the cow (gai), regarded as a sacred mother and the national animal of Nepal, is worshipped with garlands, tika and fresh grass. Cow dung is regarded as purifying and is used to clean thresholds. In the evening, Laxmi Puja begins. Houses are thoroughly cleaned, and lamps, candles and electric lights illuminate every window, doorway and roof. Rangoli (coloured floor patterns), usually made with coloured powder, rice flour and flower petals, are drawn at the entrances, and a trail of footprints leading in to the shrine represents the path of the goddess. Merchants and business owners worship Laxmi and their account books and treasuries. On this night, groups of girls and women, and in many places also boys, go from house to house singing Bhailo, the songs of Tihar, and dancing, in exchange for money, fruit and festive food.

Day 4: Goru Tihar, Govardhan Puja and Mha Puja On the fourth day, the ox (goru) is worshipped for its labour in the field, and in many households a Govardhan mound of cow dung is made and worshipped. In the Kathmandu Valley, Newar families celebrate Mha Puja, in which a mandala is drawn on the floor for each person, who is then worshipped by the family, with oil, flowers, and food, an affirmation of the sacred nature of the individual. The same day marks the Nepal Sambat new year, when processions and public celebrations occur in Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur. In the evening, men and boys sing Deusi (also called Deusire), a call-andresponse song in which a lead singer announces a verse and the group responds, accompanied by dance and blessings for the household.

Day 5: Bhai Tika The fifth day, Bhai Tika, is the climax. Sisters prepare a seven-coloured tika, placed in a row across the forehead of their brothers, and draw around them a line of oil, which is regarded as a protective circle against Yama. A garland of makhamali (globe amaranth), a flower that does not wilt quickly and therefore symbolises long life, is put around the brother's neck, and sisters pray for their brothers' long lives. Brothers, in return, give gifts, usually money, clothes or sweets. Women who do not have brothers may give tika to cousins or to male friends. The Newars celebrate this day as Kija Puja, with their own rites.

3.4 Food, Colour and Light Tihar is rich in sweets, savoury foods and fruits. Sel roti (ring-shaped rice bread) is the signature item, along with anarasa, laddu, gwaramari and many varieties of homemade sweets. A large variety of fruit and nuts is exchanged and placed in the ritual plate (thaal). The festival is also visually distinctive: coloured lights, marigold and makhamali garlands, rangoli, and oil lamps (diyo) make it one of the most photographed times of the Nepali year. Fireworks and firecrackers have also become widespread in recent years.

3.5 Tihar in Newar Tradition: Swanti In Newar custom, Tihar is called Swanti and has a particularly strong mandala tradition. Mandalas of rice and coloured powder are drawn in homes and in public squares, and the worship of Laxmi has a distinctive Newar form. The Newar celebration includes the offering of each of the five days to different beings and the characteristic Mha Puja and Kija Puja. The cultural importance of Swanti has been central to the Newar cultural revival movement of recent decades.

3.6 Critical and Contemporary Issues Gambling. The practice of playing cards, dice and games of chance during Tihar is widespread and deeply embedded, justified in popular belief by reference to Laxmi, who is said to favour those who are awake and playing. Nepalese law restricts public gambling but enforcement is uneven, and the practice remains a subject of debate. Fireworks, light and the environment. Firecrackers raise concerns about noise, air pollution, injuries and the welfare of animals, even as the Kukur Tihar tradition celebrates dogs. Campaigns for quiet and 'green' Tihar have become more prominent. Commercialisation. The festival period is a major commercial season for retailers, with significant expenditure on gold, electronics, clothes and sweets.

Part Four: The Two Festivals Together

4.1 A Complementary Pair Dashain and Tihar are often described together, but they differ in theme and in mood. Dashain is a festival of power, victory and hierarchy. Its central symbols are the sword, the goddess in her martial form, the vertical order of generations in the tika ceremony, and the state. Tihar is a festival of light, prosperity and horizontal bonds. Its central symbols are the lamp, the animals, the sister-brother relation, and the home. In simple terms, Dashain asks for the blessing of elders and the protection of the mother goddess; Tihar celebrates equality of affection between siblings and the good fortune of the household.

4.2 Shared Features Both festivals involve the cleaning and renewal of the household, the use of tika as a sign of blessing, the use of flowers (especially marigold), special foods, the return of migrants, and a surge in economic activity. Both also function as markers of the passage of the year, the end of the monsoon and the start of the long, dry season.

Part Five: The Modern Era

5.1 Labour Migration and the Festival Economy The most significant change in recent decades has been the mass migration of Nepali workers abroad. Remittances now make up a major share of the national economy, and the festival season is the most important time for returning migrants. Many families depend on the funds sent before Dashain to pay for festival expenses, and many workers who cannot return mark the festival from afar by phone and video call.

5.2 Public Holidays and Official Observances The Government of Nepal designates a long public holiday for Dashain and a shorter one for Tihar, and schools and offices are closed. Official dates are published each year on the recommendation of the national almanac authority.

5.3 The Diaspora Nepali communities in India, the United Kingdom, the United States, Australia, Japan, the Gulf and elsewhere celebrate both festivals with local temples, community associations and cultural programmes. The festivals have also become a vehicle for presenting Nepali culture to international audiences, particularly the dog worship of Kukur Tihar. 5.4 Technology and Change Online shopping, digital greetings, money-transfer apps and live-streamed rituals have become part of the festivals. Video-call tika ceremonies and digital remittances reflect adaptation to a mobile society, though many observers note that they cannot fully replace the physical presence that the rituals require.

Part Six: Chronological Summary

Period Development Vedic and early Puranic period Roots of goddess worship, harvest rites, Yama and cattle traditions c. 5th–6th century CE Composition of the Devi Mahatmya (Markandeya Purana), the core text of Durga worship Licchavi period (c. 4th–9th century) Mahishasuramardini imagery and Shakta devotion visible in the valley 879–880 CE Beginning of the Nepal Sambat era, according to Newar tradition c. 1324 CE Arrival of Taleju Bhawani in the valley with Harisimhadeva, according to tradition Malla period (12th–18th century) Dashain as a state festival; Taleju temples in Kathmandu, Patan, Bhaktapur 1768–69 Conquest of the Kathmandu Valley by Prithvi Narayan Shah; merging of Gorkhali and valley rites 1846–1951 Rana regime; large-scale state and military Dashain display.
Glossary Aunsi: new moon day Bhailo: songs sung by girls and women during Tihar Bhai Tika: fifth day of Tihar, in which sisters bless brothers Dakshina: ritual gift of money Deusi: call-and-response songs of Tihar Diyo: oil lamp Ghatasthapana: the first day of Dashain, installation of the sacred vessel Jamara: barley shoots grown for Dashain Kalash: sacred water vessel Kot: armoury; the site of the weapon-worship ritual Kuladevi: clan goddess Makhamali: globe amaranth flower used in Bhai Tika garlands Mha Puja: Newar worship of the self Mohani: Newar name for Dashain Navadurga: the nine forms of Durga Navaratri: the nine nights of the goddess Panchang: Hindu almanac

Period Development 1854 Muluki Ain legal code under Jang Bahadur Rana; Hindu social order codified 1960–1990 Panchayat era; festival tied to the monarchy 1990 and 2006 Democratic restoration and the People's Movement 2008 Abolition of the monarchy; the President becomes head of the tika ceremony Present Migration, commercialisation, diaspora celebration and ongoing debates over sacrifice, inclusion and the environment

Phulpati: seventh-day ritual of bringing sacred flowers and leaves Prasad: blessed food offering Sait: auspicious moment Sel roti: ring-shaped rice bread of Tihar Swanti: Newar name for Tihar Taleju: the royal tutelary goddess of the Malla and Shah kings Tika: ritual mark on the forehead Tithi: lunar day

Conclusion Dashain and Tihar are far more than holidays. They are living archives of Nepal's history, containing in their rituals the memory of Puranic myth, Malla kingship, Gorkhali conquest, Rana militarism, democratic upheaval and the movement of millions of people across borders. They affirm the bonds of family and the cycle of the agricultural year, while also raising enduring questions about tradition and change, about unity and diversity, and about how an ancient faith can speak to a rapidly changing society. To study them is to study Nepal itself.

audios.title: Life, Death, and the Universe - Alan Watts
audios.desc: Life is a brief moment in an endless universe. We are born, we live, and we die, while everything continues to change. Perhaps the secret is not to understand everything, but to live, love, and embrace the mystery of existence.
audios.text:
A philosophical lecture on existence, impermanence, and the mystery of being

Imagine, for a moment, that you have forgotten everything you have ever been told about yourself.

Forget your name. Forget your age. Forget your nationality, your occupation, your successes, and your failures. Forget the stories you have constructed about who you are and what you are supposed to become.

What remains?

There is still something happening. You are breathing. Sounds are appearing. Sensations are moving through your body. Thoughts are coming and going. The world is presenting itself to you, moment after moment.

Before you explain any of this, before you give it a name, life is already happening.

And perhaps this is the first mystery we ought to consider: we spend so much of our lives trying to understand existence that we sometimes forget we are already participating in it.

We look at the universe as though it were an enormous object standing somewhere outside us. We imagine ourselves to be little observers, isolated inside our heads, looking out at a vast and indifferent cosmos. We think of the stars as distant things, the earth as a place we happen to inhabit, and ourselves as separate individuals who have somehow arrived in the middle of it all.

But what if this picture is incomplete?

You did not create yourself. You did not choose the universe into which you were born. You did not invent the air you breathe, the sunlight that warms the earth, or the countless generations of living things that came before you.

And yet, here you are.

You are made from the same world you are trying to understand. The elements in your body were formed through ancient cosmic processes. The food that sustains you comes from the earth. The air entering your lungs connects you to forests, oceans, plants, and other living creatures.

You are not an object that has been placed into the universe from somewhere else. You are one of the things the universe is doing.

A tree grows. A river flows. A star burns. And, in one extraordinary corner of the cosmos, the universe has produced creatures capable of wondering about the universe itself.

That is a remarkable thing.

The mystery of being alive

We often speak about life as though it were a possession.

We say, “My life.” We speak of having a body, having thoughts, having feelings, as though there were a separate owner sitting somewhere behind all these experiences.

But look closely at the experience of being alive.

Can you command your heart to beat by conscious effort every second of the day? Can you instruct every cell in your body to perform its work? Can you consciously direct the millions of processes that keep you alive while you sleep?

Of course not.

Life is happening through you in ways that your ordinary thinking mind barely understands.

Even your thoughts arise in a mysterious fashion. You may sit quietly, intending to think about one thing, only to discover that your mind has wandered somewhere else. An old memory appears. A song enters your awareness. An unexpected idea arrives.

You can influence your thoughts, but you cannot always predict what thought will appear next.

This does not mean that you have no agency or that your choices do not matter. It means that conscious control is only one part of a much larger process.

You are participating in something more extensive than the little voice in your head that constantly comments on everything.

And much of our suffering begins when we mistake that voice for the whole of who we are.

The voice says, “I must become somebody.”

It says, “I must secure my future.”

It says, “I must make certain that nothing terrible happens.”

It says, “I must hold on to what I love, because if it changes, I will lose something essential.”

But life has never promised to remain still for our comfort.

The body changes. Relationships change. Ideas change. Circumstances change. Even the personality you defend as your permanent identity is being reshaped by experience.

The problem is not necessarily that things change. The problem is that we demand permanence from a world whose very nature is movement.

Why we are afraid of death

Of all the mysteries surrounding existence, death may be the one we find most difficult to approach.

We can speak about it scientifically. We can discuss the body, the brain, and the biological processes that sustain an organism. We can study the ways living things age and the conditions under which life ends.

But there is also the deeply personal question: what does death mean for me?

Most of us do not merely fear the physical process of dying. We fear the loss of everything familiar.

We fear losing the people we love. We fear losing our memories, our ambitions, our unfinished projects, and the experiences we hoped still to have. We fear the possibility that everything we call ourselves might disappear.

And so we try not to think about death.

We fill our days with activity. We make plans. We pursue possessions, recognition, entertainment, and achievement. Some of these things are valuable in themselves, but sometimes we use them as distractions from the uncomfortable knowledge that our time is limited.

We behave as though, if we remain sufficiently occupied, the question will never need to be answered.

But death does not become less real because we refuse to consider it.

Perhaps the more useful question is not how to escape the thought of death, but how to live with the awareness that life is finite.

Consider a beautiful song.

Would you insist that the song must continue forever, without its final note? Would you call it meaningless because it ends?

The ending is not an accident added to the song after the music has finished. The movement of the music includes beginnings, developments, pauses, changes, and conclusions.

A song that never reached another note, never changed, never resolved, would not be the same kind of experience.

Life is not exactly like music, of course, and this comparison cannot tell us what happens after death. But it can help us recognize that an ending does not automatically make everything that came before it worthless.

A flower does not need to remain in bloom forever to have been beautiful.

A conversation does not need to continue eternally to have mattered.

A human life does not need to last forever for love, kindness, courage, and discovery to have significance.

The fact that something is temporary does not make it unreal.

In some ways, its temporary nature is precisely what makes us pay attention.

What can we honestly know about death?

When we speak about death, we should be careful not to confuse hope, belief, and knowledge.

Different religious and philosophical traditions offer different accounts of what happens when the body dies. Some describe an afterlife. Some speak of rebirth. Others understand personal existence as ending with the death of the organism.

People may find profound meaning in these traditions, but no philosophical metaphor should be mistaken for conclusive proof.

There is an honest mystery here.

We know that living organisms are mortal. We know that the body is part of the natural world and that its physical components return to the broader processes of nature. We can observe how life depends on the functioning of the brain and body.

But the ultimate question of what, if anything, is experienced after death remains a subject of philosophical and religious disagreement.

We need not pretend to possess certainty where we do not have it.

In fact, admitting uncertainty can be a form of intellectual courage.

You do not have to solve the mystery of death before you can live meaningfully.

You do not have to settle every question about eternity before you can appreciate the person sitting beside you.

And you do not need a complete explanation of the universe before you can be moved by the sight of sunlight passing through a window.

There is a difference between living with an unanswered question and being unable to live until the question is answered.

Perhaps wisdom begins when we discover that difference.

The universe is not standing still

Now consider the universe itself.

Look at the night sky and imagine the distances involved. The light from some stars has traveled for years, centuries, or much longer before reaching your eyes. When you look outward, you are also looking into the past.

The universe is not a static collection of objects. It is a history of change.

Stars form and die. Galaxies move. Matter gathers into structures. Planets develop under particular conditions. On at least one planet, chemistry gave rise to life, and life evolved into forms capable of language, imagination, memory, and reflection.

Everything we know is embedded in this ongoing history.

And yet, we often imagine that the natural world should be stable while we alone are allowed to change.

We want relationships without uncertainty, happiness without sadness, success without disappointment, and love without the possibility of loss.

We want the river to carry us forward while remaining exactly as it was when we first entered it.

But the river is the river because it flows.

The universe is not a finished object. It is an unfolding process.

You are part of that process, not an exception to it.

This does not mean that every event is good, that suffering is necessary, or that we should passively accept injustice. It means that change is woven into the conditions of existence, and that a life organized around the impossible demand for total permanence will inevitably become anxious.

There is a freedom in recognizing what cannot be held still.

You can care for your health without demanding that your body never age.

You can love someone without pretending you can control every aspect of their future.

You can work toward a goal without requiring the world to guarantee success.

You can prepare for difficulties without spending every peaceful moment imagining them.

Acceptance is not the same as surrendering responsibility. It is the willingness to respond to reality as it is, rather than exhausting yourself fighting the fact that reality changes.

Are we really separate from nature?

We tend to divide the world into two categories: ourselves and everything else.

There is the human world, with its cities, languages, governments, machines, and ideas. And there is nature, with its forests, oceans, mountains, animals, and weather.

But where does nature end and humanity begin?

The materials in a city come from the earth. The energy that powers its machines comes from physical processes. Human intelligence developed through the history of living organisms. Language, culture, and technology emerged through the interactions of human beings with one another and with their environments.

Even our most sophisticated creations depend on natural conditions.

We may transform the world dramatically, but we do not stand outside the world we transform.

A human being is not less natural than a bird because the human being builds a bridge instead of a nest.

The distinction between natural and artificial can be useful, but it should not lead us to imagine that we have somehow escaped the universe.

We are not visitors who have arrived from elsewhere.

We belong to this place.

And when we understand this, our relationship with the earth can change. The environment is no longer merely a collection of resources that happen to surround us. It becomes the larger living context upon which our existence depends.

To care for the world is not simply to be generous toward something separate from ourselves. It is to recognize our participation in a network of relationships that sustains life.

The air does not respect the borders we draw on maps. Rivers do not organize themselves according to our political disagreements. The conditions that make life possible are shared.

Our separation is real in some ways, but it is never absolute.

The illusion that life begins in the future

There is another strange habit of the human mind.

We often behave as though our real life has not started yet.

We say that we will be happy when we have enough money, when we find the right person, when we move to another place, when we achieve a particular goal, or when our problems finally disappear.

We make the present into a waiting room.

Of course, planning matters. The future contains real possibilities, and our actions today can improve or damage what comes later. It would be foolish to ignore tomorrow.

But there is a difference between preparing for the future and postponing your entire existence until it arrives.

Suppose you spend ten years trying to become the person you believe you ought to be. When those ten years pass, another ideal appears. You discover a new weakness, another ambition, another condition that must be satisfied before you can finally relax.

The finish line moves.

You become so occupied with reaching the destination that you scarcely notice the journey.

The present moment is not a magical place in which all difficulties disappear. Sometimes the present is painful, exhausting, or frightening. Sometimes the most sensible thing you can do is change your circumstances as quickly as possible.

But even then, this is where your life is taking place.

You can plan tomorrow only from the position you occupy today. You can remember yesterday only through the awareness available to you now.

The present is not an obstacle between you and real life. It is the place in which every experience of life becomes available.

To notice the present is not to abandon ambition. It is to stop sacrificing every moment to an imaginary future in which you will finally give yourself permission to exist.

The self that you are trying to protect

Ask yourself what you mean when you say, “I must protect myself.”

Sometimes the answer is practical. You need shelter, food, safety, boundaries, and the ability to defend yourself against harm. These are legitimate needs.

But there is another kind of protection we pursue: the protection of an image.

We want to be seen as intelligent, attractive, successful, strong, independent, or worthy of admiration. We construct a picture of who we are and then become anxious whenever the world threatens to contradict it.

A criticism feels like an attack on our entire being.

A failure seems to prove that we are failures.

A change in someone's affection makes us question our worth.

We are no longer simply responding to events. We are defending a story about ourselves.

Yet your identity is more flexible than you may imagine.

You have been many versions of yourself already. The child you once were had different fears, desires, beliefs, and expectations. You have abandoned opinions you once considered unquestionable. You have learned things that changed the way you interpret your experiences.

And you will probably change again.

This does not mean that your past is meaningless or that you have no continuity. It means that personal identity is not necessarily a rigid object that must remain untouched.

You can acknowledge a mistake without reducing yourself to it.

You can lose a role without losing every quality that made your life meaningful.

You can admit that you were wrong without becoming nothing.

When the need to maintain a perfect self-image relaxes, something useful becomes possible: you can pay attention to what is actually happening.

Instead of asking, “How does this make me look?” you can ask, “What can I learn from this?”

Instead of asking, “How do I guarantee that nobody rejects me?” you can ask, “How can I form relationships with honesty, care, and self-respect?”

Instead of demanding that you never change, you can begin to participate consciously in your own development.

The goal is not to destroy the self. It is to stop treating every idea about the self as an absolute truth.

Love and the possibility of loss

If everything changes, then love also exists within the reality of change.

We often think that loving someone means holding on to them. We want the relationship to remain as it was when we first felt its excitement and promise.

We may try to control the other person's choices because uncertainty frightens us. We may mistake jealousy for devotion or dependence for intimacy.

But another human being is not an object we can preserve in a permanent state.

People grow. They encounter new experiences. Their needs change. Their understanding of themselves deepens or shifts.

A living relationship requires attention to the people who are actually present, not merely attachment to the people we remember.

This can be frightening because love makes us vulnerable.

To love someone is to recognize that their life matters to us and that we cannot completely control what happens to them.

There is no arrangement that removes every possibility of loss.

But if we refuse to love until we have a guarantee against pain, we may avoid one kind of suffering only by refusing a great deal of life.

Love does not become worthless because it is vulnerable.

A friendship can change your life even if it does not last forever. A conversation can give you courage even if you never repeat it. Someone's kindness can remain important to you long after the moment itself has passed.

The meaning of a relationship cannot be measured solely by its duration.

Perhaps mature love involves a difficult balance: caring deeply without claiming ownership, making commitments without pretending to control every outcome, and appreciating another person without demanding that they remain unchanged.

This is not easy. It is a practice, not a final achievement.

And it begins by recognizing that the person you love is a living mystery, just as you are.

What if there is no final answer?

The mind wants conclusions.

It wants to know why the universe exists, why consciousness appears, what death means, and whether existence has an ultimate purpose.

These are serious questions. We should investigate them through philosophy, science, reflection, and open discussion.

But sometimes the desire for an answer becomes a demand that reality make itself completely understandable before we are willing to participate in it.
Imagine that you could explain every process in the human body. Would that explanation make the experience of being alive unnecessary?
Imagine that you understood the physics of light. Would that knowledge eliminate the beauty of a sunrise?
Understanding something and experiencing it are different, though complementary, aspects of our relationship with the world.
A scientific account of music can explain vibrations, frequencies, and the mechanics of hearing. It does not make listening to music pointless.
In the same way, an explanation of the processes that sustain life does not automatically settle every question about meaning.
We can investigate the universe without assuming that our understanding will ever be complete.
There may always be another question beyond the answer we have reached.
And perhaps there is nothing shameful about that.
The mystery of existence need not be an enemy. It can be an invitation to curiosity.
You can acknowledge what you know, admit what you do not know, and continue living without pretending that uncertainty has made life impossible.
How, then, should we live?
We have spoken about life, death, change, identity, love, and the universe. But a philosophical discussion becomes valuable when it returns to the ordinary details of being human.
What does any of this mean when you wake up tomorrow morning?
It might mean that you pay attention to the people around you rather than assuming that there will always be another opportunity.
It might mean that you take care of your body without despising it for changing.
It might mean that you pursue meaningful work without making your entire worth depend on the result.
It might mean that when you are afraid, you acknowledge the fear instead of allowing it to dictate every decision.
It might mean that when you make a mistake, you take responsibility and learn rather than spending years punishing yourself for being imperfect.
It might mean that you allow yourself to enjoy a quiet afternoon without feeling that every hour must produce something measurable.
None of these things requires you to solve the mystery of the universe.
They require attention, honesty, and practice.
We cannot control every event that will enter our lives. We can, however, cultivate the way we respond. We can learn to distinguish what is within our influence from what is beyond it. We can seek help when we need it, protect ourselves when necessary, and treat others with greater care.
We can live with uncertainty without making fear our permanent home.
And we can remember that the ordinary moments we overlook are not merely the preparation for some extraordinary life that will begin later.
They are the substance of life itself.
The universe looking back at itself
Return, finally, to the image of the universe.
Billions of years of cosmic history have unfolded. Matter has gathered and transformed. Stars have forged elements. Planets have formed. Life has emerged and diversified.
And now, here you are, reading or listening to words about the universe.
You are a living being made from materials that belong to this cosmic history, capable of asking questions about the history from which you emerged.
There is something beautiful in this, even if we do not attach any supernatural explanation to it.
The universe does not need to be imagined as a human being with human intentions for us to recognize that our existence is astonishing.
Nor do we need to conclude that every event was arranged for our arrival.
We can appreciate the extraordinary conditions that made our lives possible without assuming that the cosmos was designed around our individual wishes.
You are not the center of everything.
But neither are you completely disconnected from everything.
You are a particular expression of a much larger reality, living for a limited time, capable of suffering and joy, capable of harming and helping, capable of learning and changing.
That is enough to give your choices weight.
The fact that the universe is vast does not make your kindness insignificant. The fact that your life is temporary does not make your experiences meaningless. The fact that you cannot control everything does not mean that nothing you do matters.
A small act of care can change another person's day. A decision made honestly can alter the course of a relationship. A moment of courage can interrupt a long history of fear.
Meaning does not have to be measured against the size of the galaxies.
It can be found in the way you participate in the world you actually inhabit.
The final silence
Imagine sitting quietly at the end of an ordinary day.
The work is finished, at least for now. The plans you made remain unfinished in some places. The future has not revealed what it will bring.
For a few moments, there is nothing you need to solve.
You can hear the sounds around you. You can notice your breathing. You can feel the simple fact that you are here, in this moment, living a life that is both fragile and extraordinary.
Thoughts may continue to arise. Worries may return. The mind may begin planning tomorrow.
There is no need to fight every thought or force yourself into a perfect state of peace.
Simply notice that life is larger than the commentary you have about it.
The universe was here before your personal story began. The world will continue to change beyond the limits of your knowledge. Between those two vast horizons, you have this brief opportunity to experience, to learn, to love, and to act.
Perhaps we do not need to conquer death in order to live well.
Perhaps we do not need to understand the whole universe in order to belong to it.
Perhaps we do not need to become perfect versions of ourselves before we are allowed to appreciate being alive.
We can take our responsibilities seriously without treating every problem as a catastrophe. We can love without demanding absolute guarantees. We can plan for the future while remembering that the present is not disposable.
And when we encounter the great unanswered questions, we can meet them with curiosity rather than panic.
Life comes to us not as a completed explanation but as an experience unfolding.
We arrive without having chosen the beginning. We live amid changes we cannot fully control. And eventually, each of us reaches an ending whose precise meaning we cannot completely establish in advance.
Between those mysteries, there is the living world.
There is the sky above you, the ground beneath your feet, the breath entering your body, and the presence of other beings who, like you, are trying to make their way through an uncertain existence.
There is work to do, pain to relieve, beauty to notice, knowledge to pursue, and love to give.
You may never discover a final answer to the question of why there is something rather than nothing.
But you do not have to wait for that answer before you begin to live.
The universe is not merely a distant spectacle taking place somewhere beyond you.
You are already part of its unfolding.
And this moment, ordinary as it may seem, is one of the places where that unfolding becomes your life.
